segments.text: Human Resource Management (HRM) treats employees as a strategic organizational resource — not merely as a cost of production — and covers the full “employee life cycle”: analysing jobs, forecasting how many people with what skills will be needed, recruiting and selecting them, training and developing them, managing and appraising their performance, paying and rewarding them, treating them fairly, and managing the collective relationship between employees, their representatives, and management. Each topic below is a stage in that same connected cycle, so it is worth reading them in sequence rather than as isolated definitions.

blocks.text: .2 The Role of HRM in Organizational Performance

segments.text: HRM’s strategic contribution is to ensure the organization has the workforce capabilities and behaviours needed to execute its strategy — in other words, HRM exists to serve the same strategic goals discussed under Management above, not as a separate, purely administrative function. This role is captured in the idea that people are a source of
sustained competitive advantage

when the skills and commitment they bring are valuable, rare, difficult to imitate, and well-organized by the firm’s systems — the same logic Porter’s generic strategies apply to markets, applied instead to the workforce itself.

It is important to state a claim carefully here, because it is easy to overreach: HRM contributes to productivity, quality, retention, and organizational culture, but it does not single-handedly determine organizational performance — strategy, market conditions, operations, and finance all interact with HR outcomes. A well-designed HR system creates the conditions (capable, motivated, well-organized people) under which good strategy can actually be executed; it cannot substitute for a flawed strategy or a hostile market.

The core HRM functions — job analysis, workforce planning, recruitment, selection, training, performance management, compensation, employee relations, health and safety, and legal compliance — are best understood as a connected sequence rather than a checklist of unrelated definitions:

items.text: establishes what the job actually requires before anything else can be planned.
uses that requirement to estimate how many people, with what qualifications, will be needed.
fill that need with the right people.
build the capability those people need to perform well and grow.
Employee relations, health and safety, and compliance
maintain a fair, safe, and legally sound employment relationship throughout.

segments.text: Each of the following topics develops one link in this chain in more depth.
Job analysis is the systematic process of collecting information about a job’s tasks, responsibilities, required knowledge and skills, and working conditions — it studies the
job itself
, not the performance of the particular person currently holding it (that distinction, though it sounds subtle, is frequently tested: job analysis is not performance appraisal).
Job analysis has two standard outputs:

items.text: — a written statement of what the job holder actually does, how, and why, along with the working conditions.
— a statement of the minimum acceptable qualifications (knowledge, skills, abilities, education, experience) a person needs to perform the job.

segments.text: Common data-collection methods include
observation
(watching the job being performed — useful for physical, observable work, less useful for mental or highly variable work),
interviews
(with job holders and their supervisors),
questionnaires
(structured instruments completed by many job holders, allowing broader coverage), and
work diaries/logs

(job holders record their own activities over a period, useful for capturing infrequent tasks that a one-time observation might miss). In practice, organizations usually combine two or more methods, since each has different blind spots.
Why it matters downstream:

every later HR function depends on job analysis being done well — recruitment advertisements are written from the job specification, selection criteria are drawn from it, training needs are identified against it, and even pay grades (below) are set partly by comparing the relative demands of different jobs, which is only possible once those demands have been properly analysed.

Workforce (human resource) planning is the process of estimating how many employees, with what skills, the organization will need in the future, and ensuring that supply will meet that demand. It has two forecasting sides:

items.text: estimates the number and type of jobs the organization will need to fill in the future, based on business plans, expected growth, technology changes, and productivity trends.

estimates what talent will actually be available to fill that demand — internally (through succession planning, internal promotion pipelines, and skills inventories of current staff) and externally (the state of the labour market for the relevant skills).

segments.text: Comparing demand and supply forecasts reveals a
gap
, and the gap’s direction dictates the appropriate HR response: a projected
shortage
(demand exceeds supply) triggers recruitment, training investment, or succession planning; a projected
surplus
(supply exceeds demand) triggers options such as hiring freezes, redeployment, early retirement schemes, or — as a last resort — workforce reduction.
Succession planning
specifically prepares identified internal candidates to fill key future vacancies, reducing the organization’s dependence on external hiring for critical roles.
Recruitment
is the process of attracting a pool of qualified applicants;
selection

is the subsequent process of choosing the most suitable candidate(s) from that pool. Keeping this distinction sharp is one of the most commonly tested points in this unit: recruitment builds the pool, selection narrows it.
Recruitment sources
are commonly split into:

items.text: — filling vacancies from within, through promotion or transfer. Advantages include higher motivation (employees see a genuine career path), better information about the candidate’s actual track record, and continuity; the main disadvantage is a narrower pool that may miss fresh external perspectives and skills.

— filling vacancies from outside the organization. Advantages include access to a wider talent pool and new skills/perspectives; disadvantages include higher cost, longer onboarding, and the greater uncertainty of hiring someone without an internal track record.

segments.text: Selection methods

typically include application screening, employment tests (cognitive ability, personality, job-sample/work-simulation tests), structured or unstructured interviews, and reference/background checks. Whatever combination of methods is used, good selection practice requires three properties:

items.text: — the method produces consistent results (the same candidate would score similarly if re-tested under similar conditions).
— the method actually measures what it claims to measure, and predicts actual job performance (a method can be perfectly reliable yet invalid if it consistently measures the wrong thing).
— criteria and methods are directly tied to job requirements (drawn from the job analysis above) and applied consistently to all candidates, without discrimination unrelated to job performance.

segments.text: Training
improves the skills and knowledge needed for an employee’s current job;
development
prepares an employee for broader or future responsibilities — the distinction is essentially about time horizon and scope, not about method.
A sound training cycle has four stages:

items.text: — identifying the actual gap between required and current performance/skills (often surfacing at three levels: organizational needs, task needs, and individual needs).
— setting clear learning objectives and selecting appropriate content and methods.
(job rotation, coaching, understudy assignments — learning embedded directly in real work) or
(classroom instruction, simulations, case studies — learning removed from the immediate production pressure of the actual job).

— checking not only whether learning occurred, but whether it actually transferred to improved workplace performance (a common training failure is measuring only classroom test scores, missing whether the new skill is genuinely used back on the job).

segments.text: Performance management
is the continuous, ongoing system of setting expectations, monitoring progress, providing feedback, and supporting improvement throughout the year.
Appraisal

is the formal, periodic review that sits within that larger continuous process — an important distinction, since organizations that treat the annual appraisal meeting as the entirety of performance management typically see weaker results than those that maintain ongoing feedback and use the formal appraisal as one checkpoint among several.
Common
rating errors
to be aware of when evaluating (or critiquing) an appraisal system include:

items.text: — letting one positive trait (or one negative trait, sometimes called the “horn effect”) colour the rating of unrelated dimensions.
— a rater’s general tendency to rate everyone too generously or too harshly, regardless of actual performance differences.
— rating everyone near the middle of the scale, avoiding the extremes even when performance genuinely varies.
— over-weighting recent events (good or bad) at the expense of performance across the whole review period.

segments.text: A strategic pay plan aligns compensation with job value, market conditions, individual/team skills, and organizational objectives. Two comparisons anchor a sound pay structure:

items.text: — whether jobs are paid fairly relative to one another within the organization, typically established through
(a systematic process of comparing jobs’ relative worth, often using factors such as skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions) that produces pay grades and ranges.
— whether pay is fair relative to the labour market outside the organization, typically assessed through market pay surveys.

segments.text: A workable pay system has to simultaneously satisfy motivation (rewarding performance and effort), fairness (both internal and external), affordability (what the organization can sustainably pay), and legal compliance (minimum wage and non-discrimination requirements) — these four goals frequently pull in different directions, and much of the practical difficulty of compensation design lies in balancing them.
Compensation is usefully split into three components:
base pay
(compensates the job itself, drawn from the pay structure above),
incentives
(link some portion of reward directly to results or behaviour — bonuses, commissions, profit-sharing), and
benefits

(indirect, non-cash rewards such as leave, health insurance, and retirement contributions). The design questions are the same as above: does the total package sustain motivation, remain internally and externally fair, stay affordable, and comply with applicable law and policy?

blocks.text: .11 Ethics, Justice, and Fair Treatment in HR Management

segments.text: Ethical HR practice rests on consistent rules, due process, privacy, non-discrimination, and respectful treatment. The syllabus specifically asks for three forms of
organizational justice
, and distinguishing them cleanly is a frequently tested point:

items.text: — is the outcome itself fair (was the pay raise, promotion, or disciplinary action itself a fair one)?
— was the process used to reach that outcome fair (were consistent, transparent criteria applied, and was the affected employee given a genuine opportunity to be heard)?
— was the person treated with dignity, respect, and given an adequate explanation, independent of the outcome or the process used to reach it?

segments.text: A useful example that separates all three: an employee denied a promotion (an outcome that may or may not be distributively fair) might still feel the process was fair if clear, consistent criteria were applied to all candidates, and might still feel treated with respect if the decision was explained to them honestly and courteously — showing that these three forms of justice can genuinely vary independently of one another, and a manager can get two right while failing the third.
Labour relations concern the ongoing relationship among employees, their representative unions (where they exist), and management.
Collective bargaining

is the structured negotiation process between employee representatives and management over terms and conditions of employment — wages, hours, working conditions, and grievance procedures. Beyond bargaining itself, the broader labour-relations relationship also includes
representation
(how employee interests are formally voiced),
grievance handling
(a formal procedure for raising and resolving individual employee complaints), and
dispute resolution
mechanisms (mediation, conciliation, arbitration) for when negotiation reaches an impasse. The key underlying distinction is between
individual employee relations
(the relationship and terms negotiated one employee at a time, typically through an individual employment contract) and
collective employee relations

(terms negotiated jointly on behalf of a group of employees through their representatives) — most modern labour law and much of this topic exists precisely because the collective and individual channels can produce different bargaining power and different outcomes.
Key takeaways for the HRM unit

items.text: HRM is a connected life-cycle (analyse → plan → recruit/select → train/develop → manage performance → compensate → maintain fair, lawful relations), not a set of unrelated topics — most exam questions reward showing how one stage feeds the next.

Several near-identical-sounding pairs are deliberately tested for the ability to distinguish them: recruitment vs. selection, training vs. development, performance management vs. appraisal, and distributive vs. procedural vs. interactional justice.

Good HR practice is judged by reliability, validity, and fairness in selection; by consistent, well-designed cycles in training and appraisal; and by balancing motivation, equity, affordability, and legal compliance in compensation.
